title: The heart: Two connected loops
visualTask: Follow the arrows through both loops. Separate the place where blood is pumped from the place where it exchanges gases.

title: Vessels and exchange
visualTask: Follow the red route into the fine blood-vessel network and out through the blue route. The separate green branches collect tissue fluid into lymph vessels.

title: Lungs: Exchanging gases
visualTask: Follow the oxygen and carbon-dioxide arrows separately. Then follow blood past the air sac without letting the blood route become the air route.

title: Blood: More than one job
visualTask: Compare three components with different jobs: oxygen transport, defense, and clotting. Their shapes help distinguish them, but shape alone does not show the full job.

title: Breathing: Changing space and pressure
visualTask: Follow the large airway into smaller branches. Air reaches these structures because chest movement changes pressure; the muscle action itself is not drawn here.

title: Preview: Deliveries to every cell
visualTask: Find the heart and follow one route toward a branching tissue network. What other organ must exchange gases before blood can keep supplying those tissues?

title: Review: Trace an oxygen delivery
visualTask: Trace the arrows through the lung and body loops. Identify where blood changes its gas cargo, then where that cargo can reach body tissues.

title: Brain, spinal cord, and nerves
visualTask: Compare the large upper regions with the smaller gray region at the lower back and the pink connecting stalk. Use their positions to organize their cooperating jobs.

title: Hormones: Messages carried in blood
visualTask: Find the thyroid beside the windpipe. Connect this location with a message that enters blood; the pituitary and target-cell receptors are not shown.

title: Feedback: Keeping conditions workable
visualTask: Find the green sweat gland and the red and blue blood vessels. Connect these structures with the cooling response, then consider why that response decreases as excess warmth falls.

title: Hearing and balance: Turning movement into signals
visualTask: Trace sound from the ear canal toward the coiled inner-ear structure. Contrast the coil’s hearing role with the nearby curved balance structures.

title: Vision: From light to information
visualTask: Trace light from the curved front toward the back lining. Then locate the nerve leaving the eye: the route changes from light to cellular signals.

title: Preview: Sense, respond, adjust
visualTask: Compare the nerve map with the thyroid’s position. Nerve signals follow connected cells; thyroid hormones enter blood and can reach distant responsive cells.

title: Reflexes: A quick protective route
visualTask: Find the spinal cord below the brain, then a branching nerve route. Imagine a response beginning through spinal connections while another route carries information upward.

title: Review: Information, messages, feedback
visualTask: Compare the two message routes. Use the nerve map for a movement command, then use the thyroid to explain how a hormone can act at a distant target.

title: From mouth to stomach
visualTask: Locate the central stomach space and surrounding wall. Connect mixing with muscle in the wall and chemical digestion with substances released into the space.

title: Absorption and the large intestine
visualTask: Trace a route from the intestinal space across a thin villus lining toward a transport vessel. Notice how many projections increase the crossing surface.

title: Kidneys: Filtering and keeping useful materials
visualTask: Start at each kidney and follow its tube to the bladder, then find the separate outlet. Distinguish urine production from storage.

title: Digestive helpers: Liver, gallbladder, pancreas
visualTask: Locate the green gallbladder and its ducts beneath the liver. Follow the bile route toward the intestine rather than sending a bite of food through the liver.

title: Preview: Getting supplies, removing wastes
visualTask: Trace the food route in the first picture and the urine route in the second. Notice that the kidneys are not another stop along the food tube.

title: Review: Follow a meal and a waste
visualTask: Use the two routes to distinguish stool from urine. Then identify where absorbed nutrients leave the food route and why their later transport requires blood.

title: Water balance: Changing what is kept
visualTask: Compare the two views. Skin can lose water through sweat, while kidneys can adjust how much filtered water returns to blood. Which changes would help conserve water?

title: Cells and tissues
visualTask: Compare the long extension of the nerve cell with the closely packed cells in the lining. How does each arrangement support a different job?

title: Organs and systems
visualTask: Find the stomach in the system overview, then inspect its cutaway. Notice how a single organ has internal structures and also belongs to a larger connected route.

title: Following connections
visualTask: Start at the heart in the circulation map and follow a route toward a body tissue. Imagine oxygen being delivered there while a separate nerve pathway controls muscle activity.

title: Start here: A body made of working parts
visualTask: Compare the routes in these two maps. One carries blood; the other carries nerve signals. Which route could deliver oxygen, and which could guide a movement?

title: Review: Build a body explanation
visualTask: Use the close-up and the organ picture to rebuild the levels: cells form tissue; several tissues contribute to an organ; the organ cooperates in a system.

title: Skin: Barrier, sensing, temperature
visualTask: Compare the intact upper boundary, yellow sensory structures, green coiled sweat gland, and red and blue vessels. Connect each with a different skin job.

title: Immune cells and lymph routes
visualTask: Follow the vessels toward and away from the node. Distinguish the transport route pictured here from immune-cell encounters occurring inside the node.

title: Early responses and immune memory
visualTask: Compare a physical barrier with a defense cell. Which can reduce entry, and which can act after entry? Neither picture alone explains immune memory.

title: Preview: Layers of protection
visualTask: Start with the skin’s intact surface, then compare a defense cell. A barrier can reduce entry; an internal cell response helps when material gets past a barrier.

title: Review: A barrier is crossed
visualTask: Imagine material crossing the skin barrier. Use the pictures to connect the entry point with transport toward a lymph node where immune cells can encounter carried material.

title: Living bones and joints
visualTask: Locate the skull, rib cage, and spine. Compare the elbow’s joint with the shoulder’s: which movements would their different shapes allow?

title: Muscles make tension
visualTask: Follow the muscle bundles toward the tendon. Trace how a pull could reach a bone even while the muscle holds a load without visible movement.

title: Movement needs connections
visualTask: Find the bones meeting at the elbow. Identify what this cutaway leaves out: the muscle pull and control signal needed to move or steady the joint.

title: Preview: How can a body move?
visualTask: Locate the elbow joint in the skeleton, then compare it with the cutaway. The skeleton provides orientation; the close-up reveals where bones meet.

title: Review: Explain a lift
visualTask: Use the first picture to locate the meeting of bones. Use the second to connect a muscle’s internal structure with the tendon that transfers its pull.

title: Activity: Matching delivery to demand
visualTask: Use the first figure to explain increased supply demand, then trace a delivery route in the second. The pictures show connected structures, not measurements of pulse or oxygen.

title: After a meal: Delivery and repair
visualTask: Find the intestine and liver in the digestive overview. Then inspect the pancreas separately: its digestive secretions and blood-borne hormones take different routes.

title: Final connections: Explain, predict, check
visualTask: Choose a material entering through one system and reaching another through blood. Use both maps to identify what the pictures show and what your explanation must add.

title: Preview: Explain a whole-body event
visualTask: Connect a muscle’s work with blood delivery. Which picture helps explain the pull, and which helps explain how supplies can reach working cells?

title: Final review: Tell the whole story
visualTask: Choose one scenario from this review. Use the two maps to trace a material and a separate control signal; name the connection your explanation adds between the pictures.
